objectives.text: Keep Denis Sassou Nguesso in power to 2031. He won a fifth term on 15 March 2026 with 94.82% of the vote and 84.65% turnout (official count, as reported by Chronicle.lu) after several opposition parties were suspended and the internet was cut on election day; most opposition parties fielded no candidate.

objectives.text: Refinance the debt and keep oil income flowing. Moody's raised Congo's outlook in May 2026 on a refinancing of $850 million of bonds due 2036 at 9.5%, with a tender for $575 million of bonds due 2032. Debt is about 98% of GDP, arrears about 13% of GDP (Moody's, as carried by allAfrica).

means.text: Oil as the lever. Congo is Africa's third-largest oil exporter, shipping 236,000 to 252,000 barrels a day; oil earns more than 80% of export revenue (World Bank, as cited by Al Jazeera). Moody's puts oil at about 90% of exports: the sources differ, so the share is approximate.

means.text: Several capitals at once. Al Jazeera names Paris, Beijing and Moscow among the alliances that have brought Nguesso investment; China is the main buyer of Congolese oil (36% in 2024, Coface); a pipeline between Pointe-Noire and Brazzaville, 90% Russian-owned, was approved in 2024 (Coface).

constraints.text: Oil dependence. Oil is more than 80% of export revenue (World Bank via Al Jazeera), so the budget, the debt service and the patronage all run on one commodity's price and volume. Our reading: a fall in either is the first shock the state faces.

paradoxes.text: The buyer that funds the state is also a creditor. China takes the largest share of Congolese oil exports and is a large lender (Coface), so the relation that pays the budget is also one whose claims the refinancing has to manage.

grand_strategy.reading: Sassou Nguesso's aim is to keep the system he has run for decades in power to 2031, and the oil income that pays for it is also the tightest constraint: more than 80% of export revenue against debt near 98% of GDP. He plays the great powers against each other for money and cover, Paris for aid and a long tie that also carries its own legal exposure over the family's assets, Beijing as oil buyer and creditor, and Moscow for the 2024 pipeline, and none of them is a treaty patron. The test of the next years is whether the refinancing buys enough time for oil to hold its price, and the paradox is that the buyer who funds the state is also a creditor whose claims it must manage.

stances.note: Partner, no alliance. Coface says France will stay an important partner despite tense relations, partly over the investigations into the President's family assets, which began in 2013 and seized property of his son in 2022 (Al Jazeera). Macron received Nguesso in Paris on 23 May 2025 (photo caption). Bond affinity is our reading: a Francophone colonial-era tie, with no source read calling it kin or grievance. Diplomatic relations since 16 August 1960 come from the Wikipedia index (tier 4). Confidence C: tier 2-3 sources, one Coface passage read only in a search summary.

stances.note: Partner, moving toward more business. A pipeline between Pointe-Noire and Brazzaville, 90% owned by Russian interests, was approved in 2024, with work possibly starting in 2026 (Coface); Al Jazeera names Moscow among the alliances behind Nguesso's investment. Trend warming is our reading of that deal. Bond affinity is our reading of the Soviet-era alignment with the USSR until 1991 (Wikipedia index, tier 4), with no source read saying the tie is kin. Confidence C: one Coface passage read only in a search summary, and no Russian-side source. The 2019 military agreement and 2025 contacts named in the brief were not found in the sources read.
